_readme: Well-known green-laning trips, as ANCHORS rather than as routes.
WHAT IS IN HERE, AND WHAT IS NOT
Each trip is a name, a description, and a handful of anchor points. It is
NOT a route: there is no geometry in this file and none is published. The
build tool snaps every anchor to a real, motor-legal byway in our own
rights-of-way data, and the APP works out the line on the phone using the
routing tiles the rider already has.
That is deliberate, for three reasons that all point the same way:
1. COPYRIGHT. The GPX files people post on forums and club sites are
their work, and republishing them in a paid app is theft however
freely they were shared. WHICH trips are famous is a fact and anyone
may state it; somebody's recorded track is not. Nothing in this file
is copied from anyone - the anchors are place names and the geometry
is computed from Open Government Licence data.
2. THE ROUTE MUST NOT ROT. A hand-drawn GPX is a photograph of what was
legal on the day it was drawn. Rights of way get amended and Traffic
Regulation Orders come and go, so a stored line silently becomes a
suggestion to ride somewhere a rider can be prosecuted for riding.
Anchors are recomputed against today's data every time.
3. SIZE. A trip is a few hundred bytes. The whole country fits in the
space one photograph would take.
WHY THE TRANS EURO TRAIL IS NOT IN HERE
The TET is the obvious big one and it is deliberately absent. It is one
organisation's own work, they ask riders to fetch the current GPX from
them before each trip, and a copy of ours would go stale against their
corrections - which is exactly the failure mode above, with someone else's
name on it. The app should point riders at transeurotrail.org and let them
import it. Anything else is both rude and less safe.
ACCURACY OF THE ANCHORS
The coordinates below are approximate - a village, a car park, a pass -
and are NOT presented as accurate to the metre. build_trips.py snaps each
one to the nearest motor-usable byway in the lane data and REFUSES to
publish a trip whose anchors it cannot place. An anchor that is in the
wrong valley fails the build rather than shipping a wrong route.
ADDING A TRIP
The bar is 'somebody planning a holiday would have heard of it'. Local
favourites and single lanes belong to the rider's own Plans, not here.

trips.name: Strata Florida
trips.summary: The best-known green lane in Britain, and the one people travel for. An old drovers' road over the Cambrian Mountains from the abbey ruins at Pontrhydfendigaid, with a string of river crossings that turn it from a ride into an event after rain.
trips.warning: The river crossings are the whole point and also the danger. They rise fast and the bed moves; what was ankle deep in the morning is not in the afternoon.

trips.name: Salisbury Plain
trips.summary: Hundreds of miles of legal byway over open chalk downland, and the biggest concentration of green lane in southern England. Fast, grassy and wide, with the abandoned village of Imber and the military ranges in the middle of it.
trips.warning: Army ranges. Red flags mean the range is live and the byways through it are closed whatever the definitive map says.

trips.name: The Ridgeway byways
trips.summary: Britain's oldest road, and the byway sections of it are still open to vehicles. Chalk track along the crest of the downs past Avebury and Barbury Castle, with views over half of Wiltshire and nothing modern in sight.
trips.warning: Only parts of the Ridgeway are byway - the rest is bridleway and footpath, and the boundary is not obvious on the ground. Voluntary winter restraint is widely observed.

trips.name: Peak District classics
trips.summary: The weekend that most people's green laning starts with. A compact circuit of gritstone and limestone lanes around Eyam and Hathersage, close enough together that a day takes in half a dozen and short enough that nothing is committing.
trips.warning: The most heavily TRO'd area in the country, and orders change often. Several famous Peak lanes are now closed to vehicles permanently.

trips.name: Yorkshire Dales byways
trips.summary: The best long-distance green laning in England. Roman road and drovers' track over the high limestone between Ribblehead and Wensleydale, miles at a time above the walls with the Three Peaks in view.
trips.warning: Exposed and high. Weather closes in quickly and there is no shelter on the tops.

trips.name: North Wales and the Berwyn
trips.summary: Steep, rocky and properly remote for somewhere this close to the border. The pass over the Berwyn between the Ceiriog and Dee valleys is the one people come for, with the Wayfarer memorial at the top of it.
trips.warning: Rock steps and loose surface on the climb. Not a first green lane, and not one to ride alone.

trips.name: Trough of Bowland
trips.summary: Quiet moorland between the Dales and the coast that most people ride past on their way somewhere else. Farm tracks and old packhorse routes around Slaidburn and Dunsop Bridge, and empty even in summer.

trips.name: Mid Wales mountain roads
trips.summary: The long way across the Cambrian Mountains, linking the reservoirs above Rhayader with the coast. The classic Welsh green lane holiday: a full day of unsurfaced mountain road with almost nothing on it.
trips.warning: Long stretches with no fuel, no phone signal and no traffic. Go in company and carry more fuel than the distance suggests.
